claims.text: The component's microstructure is vulnerable to hot cracking during traditional fusion-welding repair.
A WNbMoTaTi-based refractory high-entropy-alloy overlay can be deposited by laser cladding as a repair.
The deposited overlay will be thin.
Rapid non-equilibrium solidification produces refined grains in WNbMoTaTi overlay layers.
Rapid cooling produces a high dislocation density in WNbMoTaTi overlay layers.
WNbMoTaTi overlays have a distorted BCC lattice arising from interactions among atoms with different sizes and properties.
Lattice distortion creates local elastic stress fields that hinder dislocation motion and contribute to solution strengthening and high strength.
Fine grain boundaries impede dislocation motion and provide fine-grain strengthening in WNbMoTaTi overlays.
The refined overlay microstructure minimizes crack-initiation sites.
Traditional fusion welding imposes prolonged high-heat exposure that encourages hot-crack formation and produces a less refined microstructure.
The laser-clad refractory-HEA overlay will be less susceptible to hot cracking than a traditional fusion-weld repair.
The laser-clad refractory-HEA overlay will have greater microhardness than a traditional fusion-weld repair.
The tailored HEA overlay microstructure will improve high-temperature wear resistance relative to traditional fusion-weld repairs.
The laser-clad refractory-HEA overlay will improve fatigue resistance relative to traditional fusion-weld repairs.
The overlay will improve resistance to high-temperature deformation.
The repaired component can operate at temperatures up to 900–1000 °C under high mechanical stress.
The approach is applicable to critical components exposed to high temperatures and cyclic mechanical loads when only a surface repair is viable.
The magnitude of the expected improvements and long-term durability under aggressive cyclic service remain uncertain and require empirical validation.
